claim: Aberrant HOXA9 expression is a hallmark of most aggressive acute leukemias, notably those with KMT2A (MLL) gene rearrangements.
source: Aberrant HOXA9 expression is a hallmark of most aggressive acute leukemias, notably those with KMT2A (MLL) gene rearrangements.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract supported by established scientific knowledge about HOXA9 in leukemia.

claim: HOXA9 overexpression predicts poor diagnosis and outcome in leukemia.
source: HOXA9 overexpression not only predicts poor diagnosis and outcome but also plays a critical role in leukemia transformation and maintenance.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations in the introduction and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: HOXA9 plays a critical role in leukemia transformation and maintenance.
source: HOXA9 overexpression not only predicts poor diagnosis and outcome but also plays a critical role in leukemia transformation and maintenance.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the introduction section.

claim: The study generated HOXA9-mCherry knock-in reporter cell lines to dissect HOXA9 regulation.
source: Here, we generated the HOXA9-mCherry knock-in reporter cell lines to dissect HOXA9 regulation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: USF2 is a novel regulator of HOXA9 expression identified through CRISPR/Cas9 screening.
source: By utilizing the reporter and CRISPR/Cas9 screens, we identified transcription factors controlling HOXA9 expression, including a novel regulator, USF2, whose depletion significantly down-regulated HOXA9 expression and impaired MLLr leukemia cell proliferation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from CRISPR screens shown in Figure 3 and validation experiments in Figures 4-5.

claim: USF2 depletion significantly down-regulated HOXA9 expression.
source: By utilizing the reporter and CRISPR/Cas9 screens, we identified transcription factors controlling HOXA9 expression, including a novel regulator, USF2, whose depletion significantly down-regulated HOXA9 expression and impaired MLLr leukemia cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: USF2 depletion impaired MLLr leukemia cell proliferation.
source: By utilizing the reporter and CRISPR/Cas9 screens, we identified transcription factors controlling HOXA9 expression, including a novel regulator, USF2, whose depletion significantly down-regulated HOXA9 expression and impaired MLLr leukemia cell proliferation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Ectopic expression of Hoxa9 rescued impaired leukemia cell proliferation upon USF2 loss.
source: Ectopic expression of Hoxa9 rescued impaired leukemia cell proliferation upon USF2 loss.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Cut and Run analysis revealed direct occupancy of USF2 at HOXA9 promoter in MLLr leukemia cells.
source: Cut and Run analysis revealed the direct occupancy of USF2 at HOXA9 promoter in MLLr leukemia cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: During normal hematopoiesis, HOXA9 plays a critical role in hematopoietic stem cell expansion.
source: During normal hematopoiesis, HOXA9 plays a critical role in hematopoietic stem cell expansion and is epigenetically silenced during lineage differentiation (Alharbi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alharbi et al., 2013.

claim: HOXA9 is epigenetically silenced during lineage differentiation in normal hematopoiesis.
source: During normal hematopoiesis, HOXA9 plays a critical role in hematopoietic stem cell expansion and is epigenetically silenced during lineage differentiation (Alharbi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Alharbi et al., 2013.

claim: HOXA9 overexpression is commonly observed in over 70% of human acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cases.
source: HOXA9 overexpression is commonly observed in over 70% of human acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cases and ~10% of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cases (Jambon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jambon et al., 2019.

claim: HOXA9 overexpression is commonly observed in ~10% of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cases.
source: HOXA9 overexpression is commonly observed in over 70% of human acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cases and ~10% of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) cases (Jambon et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jambon et al., 2019.

claim: High expression of HOXA9 is sharply correlated with poor prognosis and outcome in human leukemia.
source: Notably, the high expression of HOXA9 is sharply correlated with poor prognosis and outcome in human leukemia (Golub et al., 1999; Baccelli et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Golub et al., 1999 and Baccelli et al., 2019.

claim: Forced expression of HOXA9 enforces self-renewal in murine marrow progenitors.
source: Forced expression of HOXA9 enforces self-renewal, impairs myeloid differentiation of murine marrow progenitors, and ultimately leads to late onset of leukemia transformation (Bach et al., 2010), which is accelerated by co-expression with interacting partner protein MEIS1 (Kroon, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bach et al., 2010.

claim: Forced expression of HOXA9 impairs myeloid differentiation of murine marrow progenitors.
source: Forced expression of HOXA9 enforces self-renewal, impairs myeloid differentiation of murine marrow progenitors, and ultimately leads to late onset of leukemia transformation (Bach et al., 2010), which is accelerated by co-expression with interacting partner protein MEIS1 (Kroon, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bach et al., 2010.

claim: Forced expression of HOXA9 ultimately leads to late onset of leukemia transformation.
source: Forced expression of HOXA9 enforces self-renewal, impairs myeloid differentiation of murine marrow progenitors, and ultimately leads to late onset of leukemia transformation (Bach et al., 2010), which is accelerated by co-expression with interacting partner protein MEIS1 (Kroon, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bach et al., 2010.

claim: Leukemia transformation by HOXA9 is accelerated by co-expression with interacting partner protein MEIS1.
source: Forced expression of HOXA9 enforces self-renewal, impairs myeloid differentiation of murine marrow progenitors, and ultimately leads to late onset of leukemia transformation (Bach et al., 2010), which is accelerated by co-expression with interacting partner protein MEIS1 (Kroon, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kroon, 1998.

claim: Knocking down HOXA9 expression results in leukemic cell differentiation and apoptosis.
source: Conversely, knocking down HOXA9 expression results in leukemic cell differentiation and apoptosis (Ayton and Cleary, 2003; Zeisig et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ayton and Cleary, 2003 and Zeisig et al., 2004.

claim: A wide variety of genetic alterations in leukemia contribute to HOXA9 dysregulation including MLL gene rearrangements (MLLr), NPM1 mutations, NUP98-fusions, EZH2 loss-of-function mutations, ASXL1 mutations, MOZ fusions and other chromosome alterations.
source: Consistent with the broad overexpression pattern of HOXA9 in many leukemia cases, a wide variety of genetic alterations in leukemia contribute to HOXA9 dysregulation including MLL gene rearrangements (MLLr), NPM1 mutations, NUP98-fusions, EZH2 loss-of-function mutations, ASXL1 mutations, MOZ fusions and other chromosome alterations (Collins and Hess, 2016a; Jambon et al., 2019; De Braekeleer et al., 2014; Collins and Hess, 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Collins and Hess, 2016a; Jambon et al., 2019; De Braekeleer et al., 2014; Collins and Hess, 2016b.

claim: DNMT3A hotspot mutations may contribute to HOXA9 overexpression by preventing DNA methylation at its regulatory regions.
source: Additionally, our recent work shows that DNMT3A hotspot mutations may also contribute to HOXA9 overexpression by preventing DNA methylation at its regulatory regions (Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2016.

claim: Genomic variation of HOXA9 including NUP98-HOXA9 fusion and gene amplification accounted for less than 2% of HOXA9 overexpression in AML cases.
source: Given that genomic variation of HOXA9 including NUP98-HOXA9 fusion and gene amplification accounted for less than 2% of HOXA9 overexpression in AML cases (Xu et al., 2016; Gough et al., 2011; Nakamura et al., 1996), uncovering the upstream epigenetic and transcriptional regulators of HOXA9 in leukemia could advance the design of novel therapeutic interventions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Xu et al., 2016; Gough et al., 2011; Nakamura et al., 1996.

claim: MLLr proteins recruit the histone methyltransferase DOT1L to the HOXA locus promoting hyper-methylation at histone H3 lysine 79 and subsequent high HOXA9 transcription.
source: For example, because MLLr proteins recruit the histone methyltransferase DOT1L to the HOXA locus promoting hyper-methylation at histone H3 lysine 79 and subsequent high HOXA9 transcription (Krivtsov et al., 2008), selective DOT1L inhibitors have been exploited to inhibit leukemia development and HOXA9 expression in MLLr leukemias and are now in clinical trials (Chen et al., 2015; Stein and Tallman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Krivtsov et al., 2008.

claim: Selective DOT1L inhibitors have been exploited to inhibit leukemia development and HOXA9 expression in MLLr leukemias and are now in clinical trials.
source: For example, because MLLr proteins recruit the histone methyltransferase DOT1L to the HOXA locus promoting hyper-methylation at histone H3 lysine 79 and subsequent high HOXA9 transcription (Krivtsov et al., 2008), selective DOT1L inhibitors have been exploited to inhibit leukemia development and HOXA9 expression in MLLr leukemias and are now in clinical trials (Chen et al., 2015; Stein and Tallman, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Stein and Tallman, 2015.

claim: DOT1L inhibitors usually act slowly and their effects remain sub-optimal.
source: However, DOT1L inhibitors usually act slowly and their effects remain sub-optimal.
evidence: This is a statement based on knowledge of DOT1L inhibitor performance.

claim: Most known HOXA9 regulator proteins are epigenetic modifiers.
source: To date, most known HOXA9 regulator proteins are epigenetic modifiers, and little is known about which DNA-binding transcription factors are involved in directly regulating HOXA9 expression in acute leukemia (Godfrey et al., 2017; Daigle et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Godfrey et al., 2017; Daigle et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2012.

claim: Little is known about which DNA-binding transcription factors are involved in directly regulating HOXA9 expression in acute leukemia.
source: To date, most known HOXA9 regulator proteins are epigenetic modifiers, and little is known about which DNA-binding transcription factors are involved in directly regulating HOXA9 expression in acute leukemia (Godfrey et al., 2017; Daigle et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Godfrey et al., 2017; Daigle et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2012; Shi et al., 2012.

claim: CTCF may potentiate HOXA9 expression through direct binding at the conserved motif between HOXA7 and HOXA9 (CBS7/9) to establish necessary chromatin looping interaction networks in MLLr AML MOLM13 cells.
source: Specifically, CCCTC-binding factor CTCF may potentiate HOXA9 expression through direct binding at the conserved motif between HOXA7 and HOXA9 (CBS7/9) to establish necessary chromatin looping interaction networks in MLLr AML MOLM13 cells (Luo et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luo et al., 2018 and Luo et al., 2019.

claim: HOXA gene expression was maintained in the CTCF-binding site deletion mutants derived from AML OCI-AML3 cells.
source: In contrast, Ghasemi et al. reported that HOXA gene expression was maintained in the CTCF-binding site deletion mutants derived from AML OCI-AML3 cells, suggesting that transcriptional activity at the HOXA locus in NPM1-mutant AML cells does not require long-range CTCF-mediated chromatin interactions (Ghasemi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ghasemi et al., 2020.

claim: Transcriptional activity at the HOXA locus in NPM1-mutant AML cells does not require long-range CTCF-mediated chromatin interactions.
source: In contrast, Ghasemi et al. reported that HOXA gene expression was maintained in the CTCF-binding site deletion mutants derived from AML OCI-AML3 cells, suggesting that transcriptional activity at the HOXA locus in NPM1-mutant AML cells does not require long-range CTCF-mediated chromatin interactions (Ghasemi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ghasemi et al., 2020 and represents an inference from the data.

claim: CTCF may play a cell-type-dependent role on HOXA9 regulation.
source: These data also suggest that CTCF may play a cell-type-dependent role on HOXA9 regulation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the contrasting findings in different cell types.

claim: The HOXA9P2A-mCherry reporter allele authentically recapitulated endogenous transcription of the HOXA9 gene.
source: The HOXA9P2A-mCherry reporter allele authentically recapitulated endogenous transcription of the HOXA9 gene and did not affect endogenous transcription of other adjacent HOXA genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The HOXA9P2A-mCherry reporter allele did not affect endogenous transcription of other adjacent HOXA genes.
source: The HOXA9P2A-mCherry reporter allele authentically recapitulated endogenous transcription of the HOXA9 gene and did not affect endogenous transcription of other adjacent HOXA genes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The CRISPR screen robustly re-identified expected targets such as KMT2A, DOT1L and HOXA9 itself.
source: Our screening robustly re-identified expected targets such as KMT2A, DOT1L and HOXA9 itself.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: CRISPR screen and global depletion of CTCF via siRNA and degron-associated protein degradation demonstrated that HOXA9 does not downregulate upon CTCF loss.
source: Surprisingly, the CRISPR screen and global depletion of CTCF via siRNA and degron-associated protein degradation all demonstrated that HOXA9 does not downregulate upon CTCF loss.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: USF2 depletion selectively downregulated HOXA9 expression in MLLr leukemia cells.
source: More importantly, we identified novel functional regulators of HOXA9 including Upstream Transcription Factor 2 (USF2). USF2 depletion selectively downregulated HOXA9 expression in MLLr leukemia cells and impaired cell growth, which could be rescued by ectopic expression of HOXA9 and its partner MEIS1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: USF2 depletion impaired cell growth in MLLr leukemia cells.
source: More importantly, we identified novel functional regulators of HOXA9 including Upstream Transcription Factor 2 (USF2). USF2 depletion selectively downregulated HOXA9 expression in MLLr leukemia cells and impaired cell growth, which could be rescued by ectopic expression of HOXA9 and its partner MEIS1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Impaired cell growth from USF2 depletion could be rescued by ectopic expression of HOXA9 and its partner MEIS1.
source: More importantly, we identified novel functional regulators of HOXA9 including Upstream Transcription Factor 2 (USF2). USF2 depletion selectively downregulated HOXA9 expression in MLLr leukemia cells and impaired cell growth, which could be rescued by ectopic expression of HOXA9 and its partner MEIS1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SEM cells have a typical B-ALL signature along with a t(4;11) translocation.
source: Therefore, we utilized our previously reported high-efficiency knock-in strategy, 'CHASE knock-in' (Hyle et al., 2019), to deliver the P2A-mCherry cassette upstream of the HOXA9 stop codon in a patient-derived human B-ALL cell line, SEM, which has a typical B-ALL signature along with a t(4;11) translocation and maintains one single allele expression of the HOXA gene cluster (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hyle et al., 2019 and data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: SEM cells maintain one single allele expression of the HOXA gene cluster.
source: Therefore, we utilized our previously reported high-efficiency knock-in strategy, 'CHASE knock-in' (Hyle et al., 2019), to deliver the P2A-mCherry cassette upstream of the HOXA9 stop codon in a patient-derived human B-ALL cell line, SEM, which has a typical B-ALL signature along with a t(4;11) translocation and maintains one single allele expression of the HOXA gene cluster (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: P2A-mediated ribosome skipping disrupts the synthesis of the glycyl-prolyl peptide bond at the C-terminus of the P2A peptide.
source: Because the P2A-mediated ribosome skipping disrupts the synthesis of the glycyl-prolyl peptide bond at the C-terminus of the P2A peptide, translation leads to dissociation of the P2A peptide and its immediate downstream mCherry protein (Kim et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kim et al., 2011.

claim: The knock-in allele produces a functional HOXA9 protein under control of the endogenous promoter and intrinsic cis-regulatory elements while delivering a separate mCherry protein.
source: Therefore, the knock-in allele would produce a functional HOXA9 protein under control of the endogenous promoter and intrinsic cis-regulatory elements while delivering a separate mCherry protein.
evidence: This is based on the design of the knock-in construct and is supported by experimental validation in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: On-target knock-in cells displayed co-localization of red and green fluorescence without random integration signals in the rest of genome.
source: On-target knock-in cells displayed co-localization of red and green fluorescence without random integration signals in the rest of genome (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: HOXA7, HOXA9 and HOXA10 were the only highly expressed HOXA genes in MLLr leukemia SEM cells.
source: RNA-seq data collected from SEM cells in our previous studies suggested that HOXA7, HOXA9 and HOXA10 were the only highly expressed HOXA genes in MLLr leukemia SEM cells (Hyle et al., 2019; Figure 1E), and that these patterns were indistinguishable between WT and KI populations, indicating the P2A-mCherry knock-in did not alter the gene expression landscape at the HOXA cluster (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E and citation to Hyle et al., 2019.

claim: Gene expression patterns at the HOXA cluster were indistinguishable between WT and KI populations.
source: RNA-seq data collected from SEM cells in our previous studies suggested that HOXA7, HOXA9 and HOXA10 were the only highly expressed HOXA genes in MLLr leukemia SEM cells (Hyle et al., 2019; Figure 1E), and that these patterns were indistinguishable between WT and KI populations, indicating the P2A-mCherry knock-in did not alter the gene expression landscape at the HOXA cluster (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The P2A-mCherry knock-in did not alter the gene expression landscape at the HOXA cluster.
source: RNA-seq data collected from SEM cells in our previous studies suggested that HOXA7, HOXA9 and HOXA10 were the only highly expressed HOXA genes in MLLr leukemia SEM cells (Hyle et al., 2019; Figure 1E), and that these patterns were indistinguishable between WT and KI populations, indicating the P2A-mCherry knock-in did not alter the gene expression landscape at the HOXA cluster (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and represents an inference from the data.

claim: DOT1L and ENL positively regulate HOXA9 expression in MLLr leukemia via direct occupancy on HOXA9's promoter.
source: Previous studies have shown that DOT1L and ENL positively regulate HOXA9 expression in MLLr leukemia via direct occupancy on HOXA9's promoter (Zeisig et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zeisig et al., 2004 and Chen et al., 2015.

claim: mCherry and HOXA9 expression were both downregulated by sgRNAs targeting DOT1L or ENL.
source: Therefore, two sgRNAs targeting the coding region of DOT1L (sgDOT1L) and ENL (sgENL) were infected into the HOXA9P2A-mCherry cells expressing Cas9. Flow cytometry and Q-PCR analysis each revealed that mCherry and HOXA9 expression were both downregulated by sgRNAs targeting DOT1L or ENL (Figure 2A–D), and that the mCherry expression correlated well with the expression of HOXA9 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–D.

claim: mCherry expression correlated well with the expression of HOXA9 in response to DOT1L or ENL targeting.
source: Therefore, two sgRNAs targeting the coding region of DOT1L (sgDOT1L) and ENL (sgENL) were infected into the HOXA9P2A-mCherry cells expressing Cas9. Flow cytometry and Q-PCR analysis each revealed that mCherry and HOXA9 expression were both downregulated by sgRNAs targeting DOT1L or ENL (Figure 2A–D), and that the mCherry expression correlated well with the expression of HOXA9 (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SGC0946 treatment resulted in a dosage-dependent reduction of mCherry fluorescence intensity.
source: Additionally, a DOT1L-selective inhibitor, SGC0946 (Yu et al., 2012), was supplemented at different dosages for 6 days to the HOXA9P2A-mCherry cells in culture resulting in a dosage-dependent reduction of mCherry fluorescence intensity measured by fluorescence imaging (Figure 2F–G) and flow cytometry (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F–H and citation to Yu et al., 2012.

claim: mRNA expression of mCherry was significantly correlated with that of HOXA9 in response to SGC0946 treatment (Pearson's r = 0.90, p<0.001).
source: Again, Q-PCR analysis of the DMSO- and SGC0946-treated cells showed that mRNA expression of mCherry was significantly correlated with that of HOXA9 (Pearson's r = 0.90, p<0.001) (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The CRISPR/Cas9 TF screen targeted 1639 human transcription factors.
source: Therefore, we combined the HOXA9P2A-mCherry reporter line and an in-house CRISPR-Cas9 sgRNA library targeting 1639 human transcription factors to identify novel regulatory effectors (Lambert et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lambert et al., 2018 and the experimental design.

claim: Seven sgRNAs spanning multiple coding exons were designed per transcription factor in the CRISPR library.
source: In this library, seven sgRNAs spanning multiple coding exons were designed per transcription factor, seven sgRNAs targeting DOT1L were included as a positive control, and an additional 100 non-targeting sgRNAs were included as negative controls.
evidence: This describes the design of the CRISPR library used in the study.

claim: Seven sgRNAs targeting DOT1L were included as a positive control in the CRISPR library.
source: In this library, seven sgRNAs spanning multiple coding exons were designed per transcription factor, seven sgRNAs targeting DOT1L were included as a positive control, and an additional 100 non-targeting sgRNAs were included as negative controls.
evidence: This describes the design of the CRISPR library used in the study.

claim: An additional 100 non-targeting sgRNAs were included as negative controls in the CRISPR library.
source: In this library, seven sgRNAs spanning multiple coding exons were designed per transcription factor, seven sgRNAs targeting DOT1L were included as a positive control, and an additional 100 non-targeting sgRNAs were included as negative controls.
evidence: This describes the design of the CRISPR library used in the study.

claim: The positive control genes HOXA9 and DOT1L were identified among the top hits between mCherryHigh and mCherryLow populations.
source: The positive control genes HOXA9 and DOT1L were identified among the top hits between mCherryHigh and mCherryLow populations, suggesting that the screening was successful (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: KMT2A was identified in the HOXA9-MEIS1 rescue TF screen but not the original screen without ectopic expression of HOXA9.
source: Among the top 10 hits from this screen, DOT1L and HOXA9 were enriched. KMT2A, the translocation partner of MLL-AF4 in SEM cells, was identified in the HOXA9-MEIS1 rescue TF screen but not the original screen without ectopic expression of HOXA9.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HBO1 (also known as KAT7 or MYST2) and several members of the HBO1 protein complex were identified among the top hits in the HOXA9-MEIS1 rescue TF screen.
source: Notably, the MYST acetyltransferase HBO1 (also known as KAT7 or MYST2) and several members of the HBO1 protein complex, which were recently shown as critical regulators of leukemia stem cell maintenance, were also identified among the top hits (MacPherson et al., 2020; Au et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the screen and citations to MacPherson et al., 2020 and Au et al., 2020.

claim: HBO1 and several members of the HBO1 protein complex were recently shown as critical regulators of leukemia stem cell maintenance.
source: Notably, the MYST acetyltransferase HBO1 (also known as KAT7 or MYST2) and several members of the HBO1 protein complex, which were recently shown as critical regulators of leukemia stem cell maintenance, were also identified among the top hits (MacPherson et al., 2020; Au et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to MacPherson et al., 2020 and Au et al., 2020.

claim: USF2 was enriched among the top hits in both CRISPR screens.
source: Most importantly, USF2 was enriched among the top hits in both screens (Figure 3B), suggesting USF2 is likely a positive regulator with less survival essentiality compared with KMT2A.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: USF2 is likely a positive regulator with less survival essentiality compared with KMT2A.
source: Most importantly, USF2 was enriched among the top hits in both screens (Figure 3B), suggesting USF2 is likely a positive regulator with less survival essentiality compared with KMT2A.
evidence: This is an inference based on the screening results showing USF2 was identified in both screens.

claim: All the non-targeting control sgRNAs were similarly distributed across mCherryHigh and mCherryLow populations.
source: Importantly, all the non-targeting control sgRNAs were similarly distributed across mCherryHigh and mCherryLow populations, indicating that the sorting-based screen did not bias the enrichment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-F.

claim: The sorting-based screen did not bias the enrichment.
source: Importantly, all the non-targeting control sgRNAs were similarly distributed across mCherryHigh and mCherryLow populations, indicating that the sorting-based screen did not bias the enrichment.
evidence: This is an inference based on the distribution of non-targeting control sgRNAs.

claim: CTCF and YY1 were not enriched in the HOXA9P2A-mCherry reporter screen.
source: Interestingly, the most-characterized looping factors, CTCF and YY1, were not enriched in the HOXA9P2A-mCherry reporter screen (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: CTCF was reported to be essential for HOXA9 expression by occupying the boundary sequence between HOXA7 and HOXA9 (CBS7/9) in MLLr AML cell line MOLM13.
source: CTCF was reported to be essential for HOXA9 expression by occupying the boundary sequence between HOXA7 and HOXA9 (CBS7/9) in MLLr AML cell line MOLM13 (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2018.

claim: CRISPR-mediated deletion of the core sequence CTCF-binding motif in CBS7/9 significantly decreased HOXA9 expression and tumor progression.
source: CRISPR-mediated deletion of the core sequence CTCF-binding motif in CBS7/9 significantly decreased HOXA9 expression and tumor progression (Luo et al., 2018; Luo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luo et al., 2018 and Luo et al., 2019.

claim: Acute depletion of CTCF via auxin (IAA) treatment significantly inhibited the protein expression of MYC.
source: Upon acute depletion of CTCF via auxin (IAA) treatment in three CTCFAID bi-allelic knock-in clones, the protein expression of a previously identified vulnerable gene as positive control, MYC, was significantly inhibited (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Cut and Run assay confirmed loss of CTCF occupancy throughout the HOXA9 locus, including CBS7/9, upon CTCF depletion.
source: Moreover, a Cut and Run assay using CTCF antibody for chromatin immunoprecipitation confirmed loss of CTCF occupancy throughout the HOXA9 locus, including CBS7/9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Loss of CTCF occupancy did not correlate with a decrease in HOXA7 or HOXA9 expression at the mRNA level in SEM cells.
source: However, RNA-seq data (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–E) and Q-PCR analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–G) collected from these three clones further confirmed the observation that loss of CTCF occupancy did not correlate with a decrease in HOXA7 or HOXA9 expression at the mRNA level.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–G.

claim: Long-term depletion of CTCF by auxin for 48 hr slightly increased the transcription of HOXA7 and HOXA9.
source: Instead, long-term depletion of CTCF by auxin for 48 hr slightly increased the transcription of HOXA7 and HOXA9.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–G.

claim: Upon washout of auxin from culture medium for an additional 48 hr, both HOXA7 and HOXA9 expression were restored to levels indistinguishable from those of the parental untreated cells.
source: Upon washout of auxin from culture medium for an additional 48 hr, both HOXA7 and HOXA9 expression were restored to levels indistinguishable from those of the parental untreated cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2D–G.

claim: siRNA-mediated knock-down of CTCF in SEM cells did not change the transcription level of HOXA7 or HOXA9.
source: Additionally, siRNA-mediated knock-down of CTCF in SEM cells did not change the transcription level of HOXA7 or HOXA9 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2H–J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2H–J.

claim: Suppressing CTCF in human colorectal cancer cell line HCT116 notably reduced HOXA7 and HOXA9 expression.
source: However, suppressing CTCF in human colorectal cancer cell line HCT116 notably reduced HOXA7 and HOXA9 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–E), consistent with the finding in MLLr AML cell line MOLM13 (Luo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A–E and citation to Luo et al., 2018.

claim: CTCF is not a key regulator of HOXA9 in MLLr B-ALL SEM.
source: Collectively, these data further confirmed the results of our CRISPR screening that CTCF is not a key regulator of HOXA9 in MLLr B-ALL SEM and likely plays a role in regulating HOXA9 transcription in a cell-type-specific manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from CTCF depletion experiments.

claim: CTCF likely plays a role in regulating HOXA9 transcription in a cell-type-specific manner.
source: Collectively, these data further confirmed the results of our CRISPR screening that CTCF is not a key regulator of HOXA9 in MLLr B-ALL SEM and likely plays a role in regulating HOXA9 transcription in a cell-type-specific manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on the contrasting results in different cell types (SEM vs HCT116 and MOLM13).

claim: USF2 knock-down significantly decreased the mCherry fluorescence in a time-dependent manner.
source: To further validate the CRISPR screen result and investigate the regulatory effect of USF2 on HOXA9 expression, we individually delivered four lentiviral sgRNAs targeting USF2 exons 1, 2, 7, and 9 into the HOXA9P2A-mCherry reporter line stably expressing Cas9. Similar to the results seen in sgENL targeted cells, USF2 knock-down significantly decreased the mCherry fluorescence in a time-dependent manner compared to that of luciferase sgRNA-targeted control (sgLuc) (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Q-PCR and immunoblotting analysis confirmed the concordant downregulation of both HOXA9 and mCherry upon USF2 targeting.
source: Q-PCR and immunoblotting analysis further confirmed the concordant downregulation of both HOXA9 and mCherry (Figure 4B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B–C.

claim: USF2 positively controls HOXA9 expression in the MLLr B-ALL SEM cell line.
source: Collectively, these data suggest that USF2 positively controls HOXA9 expression in the MLLr B-ALL SEM cell line.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing USF2 depletion reduces HOXA9 expression.

claim: USF2 was reported to generally bind to a symmetrical DNA sequence (E-box motif) (5'CACGTG3') in a variety of cellular promoters.
source: USF2 was reported to generally bind to a symmetrical DNA sequence (E-box motif) (5'CACGTG3') in a variety of cellular promoters (Henrion et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Henrion et al., 1995.

claim: Publicly available ChIP-seq data collected from human ES cells suggested that USF2 can directly bind to the conserved E-box element at both HOXA7 and HOXA9 promoters.
source: Publicly available ChIP-seq data collected from human ES cells suggested that USF2 can directly bind to the conserved E-box element at both HOXA7 and HOXA9 promoters (Cheng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cheng et al., 2014.

claim: In control SEM cells, USF2 bound to HOXA1, HOXA-AS3, HOXA7, and HOXA9 in HOXA cluster.
source: In control SEM cells, USF2 bound to HOXA1, HOXA-AS3, HOXA7, and HOXA9 in HOXA cluster.
evidence: This is supported by Cut and Run data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Upon USF2 depletion, binding occupancy at HOXA1, HOXA-AS3, HOXA7, and HOXA9 was significantly reduced.
source: Upon USF2 depletion, binding occupancy at these regions was significantly reduced (Figure 4D), further supporting the specificity of the USF2 binding identified by the Cut and Run assay.
evidence: This is supported by Cut and Run data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: USF2 could regulate HOXA9 expression as well as other HOXA genes through interactions with its regulatory elements at the HOXA cluster gene loci.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that USF2 could regulate HOXA9 expression as well as other HOXA genes through interactions with its regulatory elements at the HOXA cluster gene loci.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Cut and Run data showing USF2 binding at multiple HOXA genes.

claim: USF2 was ranked as the top 24th essential gene in MLLr SEM cells in the dropout CRISPR screen.
source: USF2 was ranked as the top 24th essential gene in MLLr SEM cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Many survival dependent genes were identified in the top 50 genes in the dropout screen including PAX5, DOT1L, ZFP64, YY1, MEF2C, MYC, and KMT2A.
source: In accordance with prior genome-wide CRISPR screens and functional studies in B-ALL, many survival dependent genes were identified in the top 50 genes in our screen including PAX5, DOT1L, ZFP64, YY1, MEF2C, MYC, and KMT2A (Gu et al., 2019; Hyle et al., 2019; Pridans et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the dropout screen and citations to Gu et al., 2019; Hyle et al., 2019; Pridans et al., 2008; Lu et al., 2018.

claim: The USF2/HOXA9 axis might play a role in supporting MLLr B-ALL cell proliferation.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the USF2/HOXA9 axis might play a role in supporting MLLr B-ALL cell proliferation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dropout screen results and proliferation assays.

claim: The proliferation-arrested phenotype was observed in all three sgRNA targeted cells against USF2 but not in cells targeted with sgLuc.
source: Next, the same assay was performed by infecting SEMCas9 cells with three individual lentiviral-mCherry-sgRNAs against USF2 (sgRNA-2,–3 and 5) at ~50% infection efficiency. As a result, the proliferation-arrested phenotype was observed in all three sgRNA targeted cells but not in cells targeted with sgLuc (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: In SEM cells constitutively expressing ectopic retroviral mouse Hoxa9, USF2 knock-down had little effect on cell growth.
source: Importantly, in SEM cells constitutively expressing ectopic retroviral mouse Hoxa9 (SEMHOXA9), USF2 knock-down had little effect on cell growth (Figure 5F), suggesting that HOXA9 is a functional and essential downstream gene of USF2 in USF2-mediated leukemia propagation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: HOXA9 is a functional and essential downstream gene of USF2 in USF2-mediated leukemia propagation.
source: Importantly, in SEM cells constitutively expressing ectopic retroviral mouse Hoxa9 (SEMHOXA9), USF2 knock-down had little effect on cell growth (Figure 5F), suggesting that HOXA9 is a functional and essential downstream gene of USF2 in USF2-mediated leukemia propagation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiment shown in Figure 5F.

claim: USF1 was also among the top 50 positive regulator genes identified in the HOXA9-reporter-based CRISPR screen (49th).
source: Interestingly, in our HOXA9-reporter-based CRISPR screen, USF1 was also among the top 50 positive regulator genes identified (49th) (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the CRISPR screen.

claim: USF1 and USF2 bind to the same type of E-box elements and are also able to form homo- or heterodimers.
source: Previously, other studies identified the USF2 homolog protein USF1 shares a similar protein structure with USF2 (49, 53). USF1 and USF2 bind to the same type of E-box elements and are also able to form homo- or heterodimers (Kumari and Usdin, 2001; Wang and Sul, 1995; Prasad and Singh, 2008; Spohrer et al., 2017) suggesting that these two proteins may function in synergy to regulate HOXA9.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kumari and Usdin, 2001; Wang and Sul, 1995; Prasad and Singh, 2008; Spohrer et al., 2017.

claim: USF1 and USF2 may function in synergy to regulate HOXA9.
source: Previously, other studies identified the USF2 homolog protein USF1 shares a similar protein structure with USF2 (49, 53). USF1 and USF2 bind to the same type of E-box elements and are also able to form homo- or heterodimers (Kumari and Usdin, 2001; Wang and Sul, 1995; Prasad and Singh, 2008; Spohrer et al., 2017) suggesting that these two proteins may function in synergy to regulate HOXA9.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known properties of USF1 and USF2.

claim: Double inactivation of USF1 and USF2 resulted in a significant decrease in HOXA9 expression compared with inactivation of USF2 alone.
source: Notably, both the flow cytometry and Q-PCR analysis confirmed a significant decrease in HOXA9 expression with double inactivation of USF1 and USF2 compared with inactivation of USF2 alone (Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A), which was also supported by a synergetic effect in the competitive proliferation assay (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G-H and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: USF1 and USF2 synergistically regulate HOXA9 expression and leukemia survival in OCI-AML2.
source: In addition, USF1 and USF2 synergistically regulate HOXA9 expression and leukemia survival in OCI-AML2 (Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B-E.

claim: In NOMO-1 MLLr AML cells, USF2 downregulation notably decreased expression of HOXA9.
source: In NOMO-1 MLLr AML cells, USF2 downregulation also notably decreased expression of HOXA9 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C) comparable to levels observed in SEM cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In human MLLr AML cell line MOLM13, individual knockout of USF1 or USF2 did not affect HOXA9 expression nor cell survival.
source: Interestingly, in human MLLr AML cell line MOLM13, individual knockout of USF1 or USF2 did not affect HOXA9 expression nor cell survival.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: USF1 and USF2 double-knockout cells in MOLM13 demonstrated suppressed HOXA9 expression and reduced survival.
source: However, USF1 and USF2 double-knockout cells demonstrated suppressed HOXA9 expression and reduced survival (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-G.

claim: Loss of one USF family member gene may lead to varying degrees of compensatory regulation of HOXA9 by the untargeted USF gene.
source: Taken together, the data suggests that loss of one USF family member gene may lead to varying degrees of compensatory regulation of HOXA9 by the untargeted USF gene, whereas loss of both USF genes results in a more robust abrogation of HOXA9 expression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data from single and double knockout experiments.

claim: Loss of both USF genes results in a more robust abrogation of HOXA9 expression.
source: Taken together, the data suggests that loss of one USF family member gene may lead to varying degrees of compensatory regulation of HOXA9 by the untargeted USF gene, whereas loss of both USF genes results in a more robust abrogation of HOXA9 expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from double knockout experiments.

claim: Upon complete USF2 depletion in OCI-AML3 and U937 cells, HOXA9 expression remained unchanged.
source: To examine if USF2 regulation of HOXA9 expression was unique to MLLr leukemias, we used two sgRNAs, sgUSF2#2 and sgUSF2#3, to knockdown USF2 expression in two human non-MLLr leukemia cell lines, OCI-AML3 and U937, which both express HOXA9. Upon complete USF2 depletion, HOXA9 expression remained unchanged, suggesting the USF2/HOXA9 axis may function in a MLLr-dependent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D.

claim: The USF2/HOXA9 axis may function in a MLLr-dependent manner.
source: To examine if USF2 regulation of HOXA9 expression was unique to MLLr leukemias, we used two sgRNAs, sgUSF2#2 and sgUSF2#3, to knockdown USF2 expression in two human non-MLLr leukemia cell lines, OCI-AML3 and U937, which both express HOXA9. Upon complete USF2 depletion, HOXA9 expression remained unchanged, suggesting the USF2/HOXA9 axis may function in a MLLr-dependent manner (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A-D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the contrasting results in MLLr vs non-MLLr cell lines.

claim: USF2 expression is significantly correlated with HOXA9 in MLLr-subtype B-ALL patients (N = 136 patients).
source: Lastly, a transcriptome analysis from the to-date largest human B-ALL transcriptome cohort (N = 1988 patients) (Gu et al., 2019) identified USF2 expression to be significantly correlated with HOXA9 in MLLr-subtype patients (N = 136 patients) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-D) highlighting that the USF2 and HOXA9 regulation axis could have clinical relevance for patients in this specific subtype.
evidence: This is supported by transcriptome analysis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-D and citation to Gu et al., 2019.

claim: The USF2 and HOXA9 regulation axis could have clinical relevance for patients in the MLLr B-ALL subtype.
source: Lastly, a transcriptome analysis from the to-date largest human B-ALL transcriptome cohort (N = 1988 patients) (Gu et al., 2019) identified USF2 expression to be significantly correlated with HOXA9 in MLLr-subtype patients (N = 136 patients) (Figure 5—figure supplement 3A-D) highlighting that the USF2 and HOXA9 regulation axis could have clinical relevance for patients in this specific subtype.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the correlation observed in patient data.

claim: The HOXA9P2A-mCherry knock-in MLLr cell line fully recapitulated transcriptional regulation of the endogenous gene.
source: The HOXA9P2A-mCherry knock-in MLLr cell line derived in this study fully recapitulated transcriptional regulation of the endogenous gene.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The CHASE-knock-in protocol is user-friendly, highly efficient, robust to reproduce and could be easily adapted to a wide variety of HOXA9-driven human leukemia cell models and other HOXA9-expressing cancer types.
source: Additionally, the CHASE-knock-in protocol developed to generate the HOXA9 reporter is user-friendly, highly efficient, robust to reproduce and could be easily adapted to a wide variety of HOXA9-driven human leukemia cell models and other HOXA9-expressing cancer types.
evidence: This is a speculation about the potential applications of the method based on its demonstrated properties.

claim: The HOXA9 cluster is located on the TAD boundary.
source: The HOXA9 cluster is located on the TAD boundary, providing an opportunity to interact with neighboring genomic elements.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of chromatin organization.

claim: The impact of chromatin interaction regulation of HOXA9 remains unclear due to low resolution of publicly available Hi-C data and lack of DpnI restriction enzyme sites within the HOXA gene cluster.
source: However, because of the low resolution of publicly available Hi-C data and the lack of DpnI restriction enzyme sites within the HOXA gene cluster that are necessary to generate high-quality 3C libraries, the impact of chromatin interaction regulation of HOXA9 remains unclear.
evidence: This is an inference based on technical limitations of available methods.

claim: Other as yet to be identified looping factors might be involved in the transcriptional regulation of the HOXA9 locus in MLLr SEM cells.
source: Therefore, we hypothesized that other as yet to be identified looping factors might be involved in the transcriptional regulation of the HOXA9 locus in MLLr SEM cells, and that CTCF regulates HOXA9 expression in a cell-type-specific context.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observation that CTCF is not required for HOXA9 expression in SEM cells.

claim: Other HOXA9-independent functions of USF1/2 cannot be excluded and requires further studies.
source: Although our study identified the regulatory function of USF1/USF2 on HOXA9 maintenance and leukemia cell survival in MLLr B-ALL and AML cell lines, other HOXA9-independent functions of USF1/2 cannot be excluded and requires further studies.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential additional functions of USF1/2.

claim: The HOXA9 reporter cells will advance many lines of investigation including drug screening and the identification of concordant epigenetic modifiers/transcription factors that are required for activation and maintenance of HOXA9 expression in leukemia progression.
source: Given the well-recognized role of HOXA9 in hematopoietic malignancies, we anticipate the HOXA9 reporter cells will advance many lines of investigation including drug screening and the identification of concordant epigenetic modifiers/transcription factors that are required for activation and maintenance of HOXA9 expression in leukemia progression.
evidence: This is a speculation about future applications of the reporter cell line.
